title: Should Pseudo-Labels Share Mini-Batches with Labeled Examples?Semi-Supervised Continual Active Learning with Limited Training Cost

paper.title: Should Pseudo-Labels Share Mini-Batches with Labeled Examples? Semi-Supervised Continual Active Learning with Limited Training Cost
paper.abstract:
Abstract Active learning (AL) reduces annotation by querying informative examples.
Continual active learning (CAL) also cuts the training cost, the total number of gradient steps, by training one model across AL rounds with a fixed number of mini-batch steps per round.
Pseudo-labels add supervision without annotation, but they increase training cost.
In CAL, where every round trains on a fixed number of mini-batches, whether and how pseudo-labeled examples should share these mini-batches with labeled examples is therefore open.
We provide the first formalization of this problem as two decisions after each query, namely (i) which unlabeled examples should enter training with a pseudo-label and (ii) what share of each mini-batch they should take.
Our method, semi-supervised continual active learning (SSCAL), works with any acquisition function.
It admits pseudo-labels based on distances from unlabeled examples to labeled neighbors, caps their share, and reweights the loss on labeled examples to keep their expected gradient contribution unchanged.
On frozen embeddings, its pseudo-labeler updates incrementally without extra model forward passes.
Across two audio datasets, two frozen encoders, six acquisition functions and ten seeds, SSCAL ranks first on average among four protocols with equal training steps, answering the question affirmatively.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Active learning (AL) selects informative examples to label and thereby reduces the annotation that model training needs. In audio, for instance, AL has studied clustering with label propagation [ 1 ] , confidence sampling [ 2 ] , and disagreement with diversity [ 3 ] . These advances target annotation efficiency. As models grow larger and deeper, the training cost, the total number of gradient steps spent over all AL rounds, becomes a concern of its own. In AL this cost also delays annotation. When the queries depend on the model, the annotator needs to wait for training in every round before labeling the next queries. Conventional AL protocols retrain for a fixed number of epochs in each AL round, so their training steps are proportional to the labeled set, which grows every round, and the cumulative cost over T T rounds grows quadratically in T T . To avoid this quadratic cost, continual active learning (CAL) [ 4 ] continues training the same model across rounds instead of reinitializing it (model continuation) and keeps training on earlier labels alongside the new ones (replay). The simplest replay in CAL combines new labeled examples with uniformly sampled earlier ones in every mini-batch [ 4 ] . Uniform replay, which samples every labeled example with equal probability, matches or outperforms costlier sampling and distillation methods in fixed-step continual learning [ 5 ] . Semi-supervised learning has long combined the supervised and pseudo-label losses within each mini-batch, with a scheduled weight on the pseudo-label loss [ 6 ] or a fixed ratio of unlabeled to labeled examples [ 7 ] . Its pseudo-labels come from the predictions of the model being trained [ 6 , 7 ] or from labeled neighbors in a feature space, by label propagation over a graph of the examples [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] or by nearest-neighbor assignment from labeled support examples [ 11 ] . Semi-supervised AL borrows this practice to also train on unlabeled examples, through consistency regularization [ 12 ] , pseudo-labels [ 13 , 14 ] or self-training [ 15 ] . In both lines of work the labeled set is fixed during training and the training cost is usually unconstrained, so pseudo-labeled examples add computation on top of the labeled ones and crowd out none of them. Inspired by both lines of work, we study whether pseudo-labels can also help CAL when every round is fixed at K K gradient steps on stochastic mini-batches of m m examples, which keeps the cumulative cost linear in T T . We call this setting fixed-step CAL. Under this constraint, pseudo-labels replace labeled supervision instead of adding to it. A round samples exactly K ​ m Km examples into its mini-batches, so each pseudo-labeled example among them replaces a labeled one. Labeled and pseudo-labeled examples thus share every fixed-size mini-batch. The displacement worsens once the labeled set grows past K ​ m Km , after which a round samples fewer examples than those are labeled, and pseudo-labels, which can be incorrect, crowd out supervision that is already insufficient. Whether pseudo-labels are worth admitting, and what share of each mini-batch they may take, thus depends on how accurate and numerous the admitted pseudo-labels are and on how much labeled supervision they displace. Without a training constraint this trade-off does not arise, so the additive gains of semi-supervised learning do not settle it. We therefore examine this mini-batch sharing in AL at an unchanged annotation budget, where labels are scarce, arrive incrementally, and change every round which pseudo-labels the labeled examples support. We formalize this problem as two decisions taken after each query and define the corresponding protocol. First, pseudo-label admission decides which unlabeled examples enter training with a pseudo-label. Second, mini-batch allocation decides how the mini-batches are shared by setting the sampling distribution over labeled and pseudo-labeled examples. We propose semi-supervised continual active learning (SSCAL), a method that works with any acquisition function. It admits a pseudo-label when an unlabeled example lies closer to two labeled positives of a class than to the nearest labeled negative of that class, caps the sampling share of pseudo-labeled examples, and reweights the loss on labeled examples to keep their expected gradient contribution equal to that of uniform replay. Its pseudo-labeler runs incrementally on frozen embeddings without extra model forward passes. Among four protocols with equal training steps, SSCAL attains the highest area under the learning curve in 202 of 240 paired runs and a mean rank of 1.18. Our contributions are (i) to our knowledge, the first study to bring pseudo-labels into fixed-step CAL, formalized as pseudo-label admission and mini-batch allocation with a corresponding protocol; (ii) SSCAL, an acquisition-function-agnostic method for both decisions; and (iii) experimental validation that answers the mini-batch sharing question affirmatively.

sections.heading: 3.1 Neighbor-margin admission
sections.text: Independently of acquisition scores, SSCAL admits pseudo-labels by propagating acquired labels to nearby unlabeled examples in a frozen embedding space, a nearest-neighbor form of label propagation in semi-supervised learning [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Pretrained embeddings tend to place examples of the same class close together, so an unlabeled example likely shares the class of labeled examples that lie much closer to it than all other labeled examples. Labeled neighbors are preferred to the predictions of the model being trained [ 6 , 7 ] because acquired labels are reliable and grow every round, whereas the model is trained for only K K steps per round and its errors would feed back into its own training [ 16 ] . On ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized embeddings, a labeled example is a positive of class c c if its acquired label contains c c and a negative of class c c otherwise. For an unlabeled candidate i i , let Δ i , c + , 2 \Delta^{+,2}_{i,c} and Δ i , c − \Delta^{-}_{i,c} be the squared Euclidean distances from i i to its second-nearest positive and to its nearest negative of class c c . SSCAL admits class c c as a pseudo-label of candidate i i when the second-nearest positive is closer than the nearest negative by a margin set by a threshold 0 < ρ ≤ 1 0<\rho\leq 1 , r i , c = Δ + , 2 i , c / Δ − i , c , a i , c = 𝟏 { r i , c < ρ 2 } , P t = { i ∈ U t : ∑ c a i , c > 0 } , \begin{gathered}r_{i,c}=\Delta^{+,2}_{i,c}/\Delta^{-}_{i,c},\qquad a_{i,c}=\mathbf{1}\{r_{i,c}<\rho^{2}\},\\ P_{t}=\{i\in U_{t}:\textstyle\sum_{c}a_{i,c}>0\},\end{gathered} (4) where r i , c r_{i,c} is the distance ratio and a i , c a_{i,c} the admission indicator. Only candidates with at least one admitted class enter P t P_{t} and thus training, since the others lack the labeled support for a reliable pseudo-label. Requiring two positives means that one mislabeled or atypical neighbor cannot admit a pseudo-label on its own, and the nearest negative bounds how far the positives may lie. Class c c is not admitted ( a i , c = 0 a_{i,c}=0 ) when fewer than two positives or no negative of class c c has been labeled, or when the nearest negative is at distance zero. For single-label tasks, at most one class is admitted per candidate, since its second-nearest positive must be closer than the nearest labeled example of every other class. The admitted class is that of the nearest labeled neighbor and is the cross-entropy target z ^ t , i \widehat{z}_{t,i} . For multi-label tasks, the pseudo-label loss ℓ i = C − 1 ​ ∑ c a i , c ​ BCE ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( x i ) c , 1 ) \ell_{i}=C^{-1}\sum_{c}a_{i,c}\operatorname{BCE}(f_{\theta}(x_{i})_{c},1) supervises only the admitted classes, each with target one, as the other classes remain unknown. Labeled examples are trained with cross-entropy in single-label tasks and with binary cross-entropy averaged over all C C classes in multi-label tasks. Labeled negatives near a candidate tighten admission and thereby bound pseudo-label errors. For class c c , suppose every candidate that does not belong to c c is at Euclidean distance at least s > 0 s>0 from every positive of c c and within h > 0 h>0 of some negative of c c . Then Δ i , c + , 2 ≥ s 2 \Delta^{+,2}_{i,c}\geq s^{2} and Δ i , c − ≤ h 2 \Delta^{-}_{i,c}\leq h^{2} , so ρ ​ h ≤ s \rho h\leq s makes the strict inequality in ( 4 ) impossible and no false positive is admitted for c c . Because admission uses only labeled examples as references, a newly acquired negative can also revoke an earlier admission.

sections.heading: 3.2 Mini-batch allocation
3.3 Incremental cost
sections.text: The frozen-embedding setting lets the pseudo-labeler update incrementally as labels are acquired. For every candidate and class it stores three distances, to the two nearest positives and the nearest negative, and each round computes distances only to the b b newly labeled examples. A round thus costs O ⁡ ( N ​ b ​ ( d + C ) ) O(Nb(d+C)) for embedding dimension d d , independent of the size of the labeled set. It needs no extra forward pass of f θ f_{\theta} and leaves the K K steps per round untouched. Table 4 reports the measured costs.

sections.heading: 4.1 Setup
sections.text: BSD10K (23 classes, macro accuracy) [ 17 , 18 ] and FSD50K (200 classes, macro mean average precision, mAP) [ 19 ] represent single-label and multi-label audio classification. Fixed train, validation and test splits contain 8,767, 1,098 and 1,091 examples for BSD10K (a stratified 8:1:1 split) and 36,785, 4,169 and 10,230 for FSD50K (the official split excluding 13 clips longer than 30 s). The annotator is simulated by the dataset labels, revealed as examples are queried. Frozen embeddings come from contrastively pretrained CLAP (Transformer, 512 dimensions) [ 20 ] and supervised-pretrained PANNs CNN14 (CNN, 2,048 dimensions) [ 21 ] , and a standard GELU MLP head d → 256 → C d\to 256\to C shared by all protocols is trained with Adam at learning rate 5 × 10 − 3 5\times 10^{-3} and zero weight decay. A run consists of T = 40 T=40 AL rounds with K = 20 K=20 steps per round and b = m = n 0 = 44 b=m=n_{0}=44 for BSD10K or 184 for FSD50K, that is, 0.5% of the respective training set. These values keep annotation sparse and training short. The labeled set grows from 0.5% to 20.5% of the training set, and the K ​ m = 20 ​ b Km=20b examples sampled per round cover it ten times in the first round and under half in the last. Each of ten paired seeds fixes the same random initial labeled set L 0 L_{0} and model initialization for all protocols and acquisition functions. As a reference from the conventional AL setting, epoch makes E = 10 E=10 passes over L t L_{t} per round, 10.5 × 10.5\times as many steps over a run. Before the first AL round, all protocols train on L 0 L_{0} , fixed-step protocols for K K steps (an identical paired warm-up, so AULC in ( 3 ) starts at the first AL round) and epoch for E E passes. The acquisition functions are random, entropy, margin [ 22 ] , Core-set [ 23 ] , TypiClust [ 24 ] and BADGE [ 25 ] , spanning uncertainty, representativeness and hybrid methods. For multi-label tasks, entropy sums binary entropies, margin averages the five smallest distances to probability 0.5, and BADGE uses BCE gradient embeddings. Entropy, margin and BADGE query with the current model, so protocols under the same seed and acquisition function may acquire different labels and the comparison covers the complete loop of querying, pseudo-labeling and training. The baselines are uniform , which samples L t L_{t} uniformly, equal , which gives sampling share 1 / 2 1/2 each to H t H_{t} and Q t Q_{t} , and new-only , which samples only Q t Q_{t} . All use the same K K steps of m m examples per round as SSCAL. The default ( ρ , β ) = ( 1.0 , 0.4 ) (\rho,\beta)=(1.0,0.4) maximizes mean validation AULC over all settings on the grid ρ ∈ { 0.6 , 0.8 , 1.0 } \rho\in\{0.6,0.8,1.0\} , β ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.4 } \beta\in\{0.1,0.2,0.4\} (Table 3 ). The main comparison contains 1,200 runs (3,120 with the full grid).

sections.heading: 4.2 Performance across settings and acquisition functions
sections.text: SSCAL significantly improves over uniform in three of the four dataset/encoder settings (Table 1 ). AULC rises by 2.00, 4.55 and 1.46 points for BSD10K/CLAP, FSD50K/CLAP and FSD50K/PANNs (paired two-sided Wilcoxon, p ≤ 5 × 10 − 10 p\leq 5\times 10^{-10} ), while BSD10K/PANNs gains only 0.17 points ( p = 0.42 p=0.42 ). SSCAL achieves the best mean rank with each acquisition function (Table 2 ), ten-seed means exceed uniform in 21 of the 24 dataset/encoder/acquisition configurations, and entropy and margin gain most, from 45.28 to 48.68 and from 46.20 to 49.64 AULC. Gains emerge early and persist across rounds (Fig. 1 ). The equal and new-only baselines, which change only the sampling shares among labeled examples, reduce mean AULC across the four settings by 0.27–1.03 and 6.59–11.30 points, so the benefit comes from sharing the mini-batches with pseudo-labeled examples. Interestingly, the epoch reference even falls below uniform on FSD50K/PANNs, so extra steps over the full labeled set do not guarantee gains even without the fixed-step constraint.

Every one achieves the best mean rank (Table 3 ), with mean ranks of 1.08–1.38 and aggregate AULC gains of 0.12–2.04 points. Increasing ρ \rho improves aggregate gains ( ρ = 1 \rho=1 still requires both positives strictly closer than the nearest negative), and a larger β \beta helps at ρ = 1 \rho=1 but not consistently under strict admission. Counterintuitively, relaxing admission lowers pseudo-label precision while improving AULC in all four settings. At β = 0.4 \beta=0.4 , raising ρ \rho from 0.6 to 1.0 lowers precision from 97.1/91.0/99.9/99.3% to 83.2/75.4/95.2/87.2% in the order of Table 1 , while AULC rises from 57.97/50.69/44.75/45.64 to 59.79/50.86/48.95/47.15. Pseudo-label precision alone thus does not predict the task benefit. At the same cap β = 0.4 \beta=0.4 , the mean sampling share α t P \alpha_{t}^{P} rises from 0.19–0.38 to 0.40 and broader admission brings more unlabeled inputs into training, so this expanded coverage and larger sampling share may explain the gains.

BSD10K/PANNs has the lowest precision (75.4%) and a neutral performance change. Precision is computed offline by replaying each configuration’s own query trajectory, so unacquired labels never enter the protocol. Relative to uniform, SSCAL adds 0.25–1.36 s of training-side wall time and epoch adds 7.43–15.95 s, so the extra time behind SSCAL’s gains stays far below that of the conventional epoch protocol.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and future direction
sections.text: We formalize pseudo-label admission and mini-batch allocation in fixed-step CAL, define its protocol, and answer the sharing question affirmatively. The acquisition-function-agnostic SSCAL method improves 21 of 24 audio configurations and ranks best on average under all six acquisition functions. Future work could extend SSCAL to end-to-end training, refreshing distances as the embeddings change.

sections.heading: 6 Compliance with Ethical Standards
sections.text: This study is limited to computational analysis of the existing public BSD10K [ 17 ] and FSD50K [ 19 ] datasets. No new experiments involving human or animal subjects were conducted.
